week_headline: Poison control calls surge as dangerous supplement misinformation spreads amid measles fears

top10.claim: Poison center reports rose 39 % after supplement was touted as measles cure
top10.verdict: No supplement has been shown to cure measles — the MMR vaccine is the only proven protection, with decades of safety data behind it. The 39% spike in poison center reports is real and deeply concerning, and it reflects what happens when unverified health claims spread faster than facts. If someone you know has been exposed to measles, the right call is a doctor, not a supplement aisle.
top10.verdict_highlight: No supplement cures measles — MMR vaccine does
sources: NIH – National Poison Control Center Data
JAMA – Vaccine Efficacy and Safety Reviews
top10.global_opinion: In the US, poison control centers have flagged this trend explicitly, linking social media misinformation to the spike in supplement misuse calls. The UK's NHS and UKHSA have issued firm reminders that measles has no cure outside of supportive care and that vaccination remains the only reliable prevention. In parts of Europe and the Global South where measles outbreaks are more frequent, health authorities emphasise vaccination campaigns heavily and treat supplement cure claims as a serious public health communication threat.
top10.brit_take: Britain watched measles make a quiet comeback when vaccination rates dipped, so the idea of swapping the MMR jab for a supplement from a wellness influencer is, to put it gently, not going to go down well with the GP. We've been here before — the vaccine works, the supplement doesn't, and the poison control line is not how anyone wants to spend a Tuesday.
